en: I worship Hari, who is the abode of the five glorious syllables, radiant with His specific attributes, yet free from all counter-correlates and devoid of distinctions. The Gopālatāpinī Upaniṣad.
I worship Hari, the abode of the five glorious syllables, resplendent with His specific qualities, yet liberated from all opposites and free from all distinctions.
Oṃ! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O worshipful ones.
May we praise you with steady limbs and bodies; may we attain that life-span ordained by the gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the all-knowing, grant us well-being.
May Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are uninjured, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
The Gopālatāpana, Kṛṣṇa, Yājñavalkya, Varāhaka, Śāṭyāyanī, Hayagrīva, Dattātreya, and the Gāruḍa.
Om, Hari! Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, whose actions are effortless, who is known through the Vedānta, who is the Guru, and the witness of the intellect.
The sages indeed said to a Brāhmaṇa: "Who is the supreme deity? From what does death fear?
By the knowledge of what does everything become known? By what does this universe transmigrate?
To that, the Brāhmaṇa replied: "Kṛṣṇa is indeed the supreme divinity."
Death fears Govinda. Through the knowledge of Gopījanavallabha, this is understood:
"Svāhā, this entire universe wanders [in saṃsāra]. Regarding this, they said: "Who is Kṛṣṇa? And who is that Govinda? Who is Gopījanavallabha? And who is Svāhā? The Brāhmaṇa said to them:

The remover of evil, known through the Vedas as the Cow and the Earth, the impeller of the entire collection of knowledge for the cowherd women, and His Māyā—all this is indeed the Supreme Brahman alone. He who meditates upon Him, tastes Him, and worships Him becomes immortal. They said: "What is that form? What is the tasting? Or what is it?"
"Tell me all about that worship for those who desire to know it. Hairaṇya said:
"That [worship] revolves around the cowherd-dress, which is cloud-like and rests upon the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma). Regarding this, there are these verses:"

The Lord has eyes like beautiful white lotuses, possesses the luster of a cloud, and wears garments as bright as lightning; he is two-armed, enriched with the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā), and adorned with a garland of forest flowers. || 1 ||
Surrounded by cowherds, cowherdesses, and cattle, seated beneath a celestial tree,
adorned with divine ornaments, and situated in the midst of a jeweled lotus.
By meditating in one's mind upon Kṛṣṇa, who is served by breezes mingling with the waves of the waters of the Kālindī, one is liberated from the cycle of worldly existence. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, its tongue is water and earth; its emissions are [the syllables] *kāmādi*, *kṛṣṇāya* as the first word, *govindāya* as the second, *gopījana* as the third, *vallabha* as the fourth, and *svāhā* as the fifth. Reciting these five words, one [protects] the five limbs, heaven and earth.
The sun and the moon attain the state of Brahman by means of that form. Regarding this, there is this verse:
"Taking *klīm* at the beginning, one should recite *kṛṣṇāya govindāya gopījanavallabhāya*, composed by the great Mānava Vyāsa; for him who does so, there is a swift goal, and no other."

"May there be a goal. Devotion (*bhakti*) is the act of worshiping Him. This consists of directing the mind toward Him through detachment from the conditions of this world and the next. And this very thing is *naiṣkarmya* (freedom from action).
"The wise worship that Kṛṣṇa in many ways."
They propitiate Govinda, who exists manifoldly.
The Beloved of the Gopīs, resting on Svāhā and possessing divine seed, sustains these worlds and this entire universe. || 1 ||
Just as the single wind, having entered the world, assumes five forms among various beings,
so too Kṛṣṇa, though one, [assumes many forms] for the sake of the welfare of the world.
Through sound, this five-footed one shines forth. Thus [it is said].

They said, "Tell us the mode of worship for this Supreme Self, Govinda, the support of all. He spoke to them: "His seat is a golden lotus with eight petals; within that is a pair of fire-weapon syllables (*adhikānalāstra*); and within that is the primordial syllable (*ādyarṇa*), the seed of all, [ending] with *kṛṣṇāya*."

Taking the Brāhmaṇa [text] enriched with the seed-syllable *namaḥ* along with Brahmā, having correctly inscribed the Anaṅga-Gāyatrī, and having fashioned a circle of the earth encircled by tridents, one should surround it with the limbs (aṅgas), Vāsudeva and others, his own Śaktis such as Rukmiṇī and others, Nanda and others, Vasudeva and others, Arjuna and others, and the treasures (nidhis) and so forth.

One should worship at the junctions of time (sandhyās) with acts of devotion and ritual services; by that, everything of his becomes complete, everything becomes complete. Regarding this, there are these verses:
"The one controller, all-pervading, Kṛṣṇa, the adorable..."
Though being one, he who shines forth in many ways— that sacred seat (pīṭha) which the wise ones worship; for them there is eternal perfection, and not for others.
The eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious,
the one who ordains the desires of the many—
those wise ones who worship Him seated upon the throne.
For them there is eternal happiness, and not for others.
For those who are constantly diligent and worship that supreme abode of Viṣṇu without desire,
He, in the form of a cowherd, [reveals Himself] through their effort.
One should reveal that very state of the Self.
To him who created Brahmā in the beginning,
and who protected that knowledge for him— Kṛṣṇa; to that God, the light of self-knowledge...
One who desires liberation should go for refuge.
To those who recite the five-word mantra of Govinda with the syllable *oṃ* interspersed,
He reveals His own form.
Therefore, one who desires liberation should practice constant tranquility. || 7 ||
From this very fivefold [lineage] arose the Manavas of Govinda among the Manavas;
they too, beginning with Daśārṇa, were born from those beginning with Saṃkrandana.
They are practiced correctly by those desiring prosperity. || 8 ||
They asked him, and he said: "While I was wandering in the abode of Brahmā, the Supreme Lord was meditated upon and praised by me;
at the end of a *parārdha*, He became manifest. Then that Person, the teacher of knowledge, appeared before me. Thereupon, I bowed down to Him, who is favorable toward His devotees."

Having bestowed upon me, for the sake of creation, the form consisting of eighteen syllables through my heart, he vanished. Then, as I desired to create again, those [syllables] appeared before me. Having divided the future form of the universe among those syllables, I manifested it.
Thus, from the earth at a certain time fire [arose], from the drop the moon, and from their union the sun;

from the syllable *klīm* the eternal sky, from the ether the wind, and from the north the fragrant sciences (*vidyās*)—I have manifested them, I have brought them forth. From that, following the north, the distinctions of female, male, and so forth [emerged].
"This entire world is this [Brahman]; this entire world is this [Brahman]. || 3 ||

By the sacrifice of this very [mantra], Candradhvaja, having dispelled delusion, makes himself known. One should repeat the mantra beginning with *Oṃ*. Free from attachment, he attained [realization]. "The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, like an eye extended in the sky."
Therefore, one should constantly repeat this; one should constantly cause it to revolve. ||4||
Regarding this, some say that from the first foot [of the mantra] comes the earth, from the second foot water, from the third foot fire, from the fourth foot air, and from the final foot space; thus,
the Vaiṣṇava mantra consisting of the five vyāhṛtis is the illuminator of Kṛṣṇa.
One should constantly repeat this for the sake of attaining isolation; one should constantly repeat it. || 5 ||
In this regard, there are these verses: From its first part, the earth [arose]; from the second, that which is born of water;
from the third, fire was produced; and from the fourth, the bearer of fragrance (the wind). || 1 ||
One should practice that very same fifth, the arising of the ether;
thus Candradhvaja went to the supreme, imperishable state of Viṣṇu.
Then that very state, which consists of five stages, is pure, stainless, free from sorrow, and devoid of all attachment such as greed.
He is Vāsudeva, than whom nothing else exists. || 3 ||

I, the host of Maruts, shall perpetually praise with the highest hymn that one Govinda, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, who consists of five parts, and who sits beneath the trees of Vrindavana.
Oṃ, salutations to the one whose nature is the universe, the cause of the universe’s preservation and end;
repeated salutations to Govinda, the Lord of the universe and the universe itself. || 1 ||
Salutations to the one whose form is consciousness, whose nature is supreme bliss;
salutations again and again to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Gopīs, Govinda. || 2 ||
Homage to the lotus-eyed one; homage to the one garlanded with lotuses; homage to the one whose navel is a lotus; homage to the Lord of Kamalā. 3.
Salutations again and again to Govinda, who is delightful with a crest of peacock feathers, whose intellect is unimpeded, and who is the swan in the mind-lake of Ramā. || 4 ||
Salutations to the destroyer of the lineage of Kaṃsa, the slayer of Keśin and Cāṇūra, the one worthy of praise by the bull-bannered god, the charioteer of Arjuna. || 5 ||
To the cowherd who delights in the sound of the flute, the crusher of serpents,
who wanders along the banks of the Yamunā, and who wears swaying earrings.
Salutations again and again to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who wears a garland of lotus-faces with faces like tender sprouts, who is skilled in the art of dance, and who protects those who bow before him. || 7 ||
Salutations to the destroyer of sins, to the upholder of Govardhana,
to the ender of Pūtanā’s life, and to the taker of Tṛṇāvarta’s breath.
Salutations again and again to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is partless, free from delusion, pure, the enemy of impurity, non-dual, and the Great One.
Be gracious, O Supreme Bliss; be gracious, O Supreme Lord.
O Master, lift me up, for I have been bitten by the serpent of mental and physical afflictions.
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, beloved of Rukmiṇī, who captivates the hearts of the gopīs;
O Teacher of the World, lift me up, for I am submerged in the ocean of worldly existence. 11.
O Keśava, remover of afflictions, O Nārāyaṇa, O Janārdana!
O Govinda, supreme bliss, O Mādhava, lift me up!

Then, having been thus propitiated with hymns of praise, Hiraṇyagarbha said: "In that way, you shall cross over the cycle of worldly existence by chanting this five-word mantra while meditating upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Whoever would cause another to recite this five-word mantra for one who is suffering...

That supreme state is reached effortlessly; it is motionless, one, swifter than the mind, and even the gods could not overtake it as it moved on before them. Therefore, Kṛṣṇa alone is the supreme deity;
one should meditate upon him, relish him, worship him, and devote oneself to him.
Oṃ tat sat—thus ends the Upaniṣad.
Oṃ! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O worshipful ones.
With steady limbs and bodies, may we praise you; may we attain the lifespan ordained by the gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the all-knowing, grant us well-being.
May Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are uninjured, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
Thus ends the Gopālapūrvatāpinī Upaniṣad.
Oṃ. Once, after having spent the night full of desire, the women of Vraja spoke to Kṛṣṇa, the cowherd and Lord of All. Kṛṣṇa said to them, "Alms should be given to such-and-such a brāhmaṇa."
"Regarding Durvāsas: how shall we cross the waters of the Yamunā?
For if we say, 'O Kṛṣṇa, may it be well with you,' the religious student will grant us a path—by remembering me, even the unfathomable becomes fathomable."
Remembering me, the impure becomes pure; remembering me, the one who has not taken vows becomes one who has taken vows; remembering me, the one with desires becomes free from desire;
remembering me, the one unlearned in the Vedas becomes learned in the Vedas—me, [remembering me...]
Having remembered, even an unfathomable river becomes fordable for everyone, though it lacks a bottom; indeed,
having heard those terrible words and remembering them, and having crossed by means of those words,
he went to that most meritorious hermitage of Sūryā and bowed to the sage.
"For this is indeed most excellent and belongs to Rudra. Having given to that Brahmin milk and ghee— which are most desired and most refined—
he, being satisfied, bathed, ate, left over the remainder, prepared the food, and having understood it, gave it.

"How shall we go, having crossed the Saurī? He, the sage, said, "By remembering me, Durvāsas, he will grant you the way. Among them, Gāndharvī, who was indeed the most excellent, spoke thus to him on their behalf: "How then, O Kṛṣṇa..."
The student: How is the sage Durvāsana?

For they, having first established that as primary, remained silent without performing [the ritual] subsequently. Space possesses sound; it is distinct from both sound and space. Space resides in that; it resides in space.
For that space does not know it; for that is the Self.
How can I be an enjoyer? This form-possessing fire is distinct from both form and fire. Fire abides in it; fire abides in fire; fire [knows] it.
He does not know; for he is the Self. How can I be an enjoyer? Water, though possessing taste, is distinct from taste and water; it abides within them.
Earth, though possessing smell, is distinct from smell and earth; it abides within them.

It stands upon the earth; the earth does not know it, for that is the Self. [The Self thinks: "How am I the enjoyer? For it is by the mind alone that one perceives this, and by the mind alone that one grasps these. But where everything has become the Self alone, there how could one perceive, or how could one go?
For that is the Self. How am I the enjoyer? This indeed is Kṛṣṇa, who is most beloved and who becomes the cause of the two bodies. There are two birds;
I am born of Brahman, while the other is the enjoyer. For the other is the witness.

It comes to be so. Those two abide in the nature of the tree; they are the enjoyer and the non-enjoyer. For the former is the enjoyer, while the other is the non-enjoyer, being black. Where we do not perceive knowledge and ignorance—how can he who is distinct from both knowledge and ignorance, and consists of pure knowledge, be an object?
Thus it is said: "He who indeed desires desires through desire becomes one possessed of desire;

he who indeed desires desires without desire becomes free from desire. This one, distinct from birth and old age, is a pillar; he is uncuttable—this one who dwells in the sun, this one [who dwells in the moon]."
"He stands among the cows; he who protects the cowherds; he who stands among all the gods;
he who is praised by all the gods; he who, having entered into all beings, ordains all beings—he indeed becomes your master. Thus spoke Gāndharvī.
How was he born among us as a cowherd, and how did you, O Sage, come to know this Kṛṣṇa?
What is his mantra, and what is his abode? How was he born of Devakī? Who is his wife and village? Of what nature is the worship of this Gopāla? He is the manifest Prakṛti.
"How indeed did this Supreme Self, Gopāla, descend upon the earth?

Thus the daughter of the Gandharva spoke to the sage. He said to her: "Formerly, from the heart-lotus of Nārāyaṇa—in whom all worlds are woven like warp and woof—the Lotus-born One was born; having performed intense penance,"

He granted him a boon. He chose the right to ask any question he desired. He granted it to him. Then the Lotus-born One said: "Among all the incarnations (*avatāras*), which one is the most excellent? By which do the worlds become satisfied? Remembering whom are they liberated?"
They arise from this saṃsāra. Or how does the Brahman-nature of this incarnation come about?
He said: "Indeed, that is the god Nārāyaṇa. Just as there are seven cities on the peak of Meru that are both with desire (sakāmyā) and without desire (niṣkāmyā), so too are those with desire."

In the wheel of the earth-protector (Gopāla), there are seven cities. Among them, Gopālapurī is the manifest abode of Brahman. It belongs to all the gods and all beings, whether they act with desire or without desire. Now follows its worship, just as indeed in a lake...

The lotus stands there, and likewise it stands upon the ground. Mathurā is protected by the discus; therefore, it is the city of the cowherds (Gopālapurī). There is Bṛhadvana and Bṛhadvana; Madhu’s [grove] is Madhuvana;
Tāla is Tālavana; Kāmya is Kāmyavana; Bahulā is Bahulavana; and Kumuda.
The city is surrounded by these: Kumudavana, Khadira, Khadiravana, Bhadra, Bhadravana, Bhāṇḍīra (which is Bhāṇḍīravana), Śrīvana, Lohavana, and Vṛndāvana.
There, within those very celestial realms, dwell gods, humans, Gandharvas, and Nāgas.
Kinnaras sing and dance. Therein are the twelve Ādityas, the eleven Rudras, the eight Vasus, the seven Munis, Brahmā, and Nārada; and five Vināyakas:
Vīreśvara, Rudreśvara, Ambikeśvara, Gaṇeśvara, and Nīlakaṇṭheśvara Viśveśvara.
Gopāleśvara and Bhadreśvara—these eight, along with others, constitute twenty-four liṅgas.
There are two forests: Kṛṣṇavana and Bhadravana. Between them lie twelve sacred and most meritorious forests; in these very places dwell the gods and the Siddhas who have attained perfection.

For therein, there is the Rāma-form of Rāma, the Pradyumna-form of Pradyumna, the Aniruddha-form of Aniruddha, and the Kṛṣṇa-form of Kṛṣṇa. Thus, there are twelve forms in the forests and likewise in Mathurā. Indeed, the Rudras worship one; Brahmā worships the second.
They worship the third [night] as born of Brahmā; they worship the fourth as the Maruts; they worship the fifth as the Vināyakas;
and they worship the sixth as the Vasus. The sages worship the seventh; the Apsarases worship the ninth; the tenth indeed stands in concealment; and the eleventh—
She follows her own path; she abides on the twelfth stage (*bhūmi*). Indeed, those who worship her cross over death;
they obtain liberation. They cross over the suffering consisting of the threefold affliction—namely, conception, birth, old age, and death. On this matter, there are also these verses:

Having reached the beautiful Mathurā, which is eternally worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods, and which is protected by the conch, discus, mace, Śārṅga bow, and the club and other weapons; || 1 ||
Therein dwells that Lord Kṛṣṇa, concentrated with his powers along with women,
together with Ramā, Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Rukmiṇī.

The word "catuḥ" (four) is indeed one, and it is declared to be the syllable *oṃ*. From that very [syllable], one should ascertain the Self as "so 'ham" (that am I), and thus meditate: "I am Gopāla. He attains liberation; he reaches the state of Brahman; he becomes a knower of Brahman.

He takes the cowherds and their dependents as his own self until the end of creation. That Gopāla is indeed *Oṃ*. *Tatsat so'ham* (That, Being, I am). The Supreme Brahman, whose essence is Kṛṣṇa, whose nature is the unity of eternal bliss—that am I. *Tatsadgopālo'hameva* (That, Being, Gopāla, I alone am). The Supreme...

Taking as his own self that which is true and uncontradicted—namely, "I am He"—one should effect a unity through the mind. One should contemplate the Self as "I am Gopāla. That very one is the unmanifest, infinite, and eternal Gopāla.
O Brahmin, my residence shall always be in Mathurā.
Indeed, [he is the one] who bears the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, and the forest garland. || 1 ||
He whose own nature is the supreme light of universal form, yet devoid of all material form—
whether he resides within the district of Mathurā or even in Jambūdvīpa— [he attains liberation].
He who worships both my image and myself is most dear to me on earth; established within that image in the form of Kṛṣṇa, I am always to be worshipped by you.
And people who follow the [successive] ages, being wise, worship me here in this world according to the fourfold distinction of my descent.
He is Kṛṣṇa with his younger brother Gopāla, intent upon Rukmiṇī;
I am the unborn and eternal Gopāla, and I am the ancient Pradyumna. || 5 ||
"I am Rāma, I am Aniruddha"— thus the wise man should worship himself according to the desireless dharma taught by me, in its proper divisions.
Indeed, I am to be worshipped by those inhabitants of Bhadrakṛṣṇa;
for those who have fallen away from that path of dharma are solely devoted to me.
Those who have indeed been swallowed by Kali, their abiding place is in her,
just as you are with your sons and just as Rudra is with his attendants.
"As I am endowed with Śrī, so is my devotee dear to me.
He [Brahmā] said: "How can there be one God when there are four gods?
How has that which is renowned as the single syllable (akṣara) become manifold syllables?"
He said: "In the beginning, indeed, there was that one alone, Brahman, without a second. From that arose the unmanifest, the single syllable (akṣara). From that syllable came the Great (mahat);
from the Great, the ego (ahaṅkāra); and from that ego, the five subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi)."
From them [arose] the elements; by them the Imperishable is enveloped.
I am that Imperishable, this syllable Om—undecaying, immortal, fearless, and deathless—for Brahman is indeed fearlessness. I am liberated; I am the Imperishable.
It is pure existence, the very nature of consciousness, luminous, and all-pervading. || 9 ||
Brahman is indeed one and non-dual, yet through Māyā it appears as a fourfold [manifestation];
Viśva, the son of Rohiṇī, is born from the syllable 'A'.
Pradyumna, whose nature is taijasa, arises from the syllable *u*;
Aniruddha, whose nature is prājña, arises from the syllable *m*.
Kṛṣṇa, who consists of half a mora, is that in which the universe is established;
Rukmiṇī is the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), whose essence is Kṛṣṇa and who is the creator of the world.
Born from the women of Vraja and endowed with knowledge through the Vedas,
the exponents of Brahman declare his nature to be that of the *praṇava*.
Therefore, Gopāla, who is established as the universe, is born from the syllable Oṃ;
the exponents of Brahman declare that *klīm* is the single essence of the syllable Oṃ.
By meditating especially upon me in Mathurā, one attains liberation;
there resides the eight-petaled, blossomed heart-lotus. || 15 ||
His two feet were marked with divine banners and parasols;
on his chest was the Śrīvatsa emblem, and he was endowed with the Kaustubha gem, radiant with light.
Four-armed, equipped with the conch, the discus, the Śārṅga bow, the lotus, and the mace; his arms adorned with beautiful armlets and his neck graced by a splendid garland. || 17 ||
He wears a radiant crown, is free from fear, and has shimmering crocodile-shaped earrings;
his golden body is gentle, and he bestows fearlessness upon his own devotee.
One should constantly meditate in the mind upon me as the bearer of the flute and horn,
or upon that by which the entire world is churned through the knowledge of Brahman.
Whatever constitutes my very essence is called Mathurā;
by the eight guardians of the directions, this lotus of the earth has been made to bloom throughout the world.
Born from the ocean of saṃsāra, it was served within my mind;
there were divine banners with the luster of the moon and sun, and Mount Meru made of gold.
The sunshade is said to extend as far as the world of Brahmā, and his foot is remembered as being above that;
moreover, the nature of the Śrīvatsa exists along with its characteristic marks.
Therefore, it is called the Śrīvatsa mark by the exponents of Brahman,
because of that [mark] which, in its own essential form, possesses the splendor of the sun, fire, speech, and the moon.
Those who consider themselves masters of speech say that the jewel named Kaustubha exists [therein];
likewise, Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas, as well as the four-armed Ahaṃkāra, exist.
The conch, composed of the five elements, situated upon the dust in the hand, is called the mind-wheel (manascakra), ending with the form of a child. || 25 ||
The primordial Māyā is the Śārṅga bow, and the universal lotus rests in my hand;
the primordial Vidyā is the mace, which is ever present in my hand as that which is to be known.
The neck is said to be devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), yet it is adorned with divine armlets of dharma, artha, and kāma, fashioned from the divine and impelled by the primordial, unconquered power.
O Brahmā, my garland is proclaimed by your mind-born sons;
they call me the immutable one, whose form is pure goodness (sattva), and the Diadem. (28)
One should constantly meditate upon my beloved, who is radiant with a pair of earrings shimmering with an abundance of milk; such a person attains liberation. (29)
He becomes liberated; indeed, I shall grant my own self to him.
All this that is yet to come has been told by me to you, O Creator.
And its own nature is indeed twofold: consisting of qualities (saguṇa) and devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
The Lotus-born One said: "Regarding the individual forms that have been described, how do their ornaments come to be? How do the gods perform sacrifice? How do the Rudras perform sacrifice?
How does Brahmā perform sacrifice? How do those born of Brahmā perform sacrifice? How do the Vināyakas perform sacrifice? [And] the twelve Ādityas?"

The Vasus sacrifice; the Gandharvas sacrifice. With their followers, they stand in concealment. What do human beings sacrifice? He said to him: "Indeed, those twelve primordial and manifest forms of the divine Nārāyaṇa exist in all worlds and in all [beings]."
She abides among all the gods and among men: as Raudrī among the Rudras, Brāhmī among the Brahmās, Daivī among the gods, Mānavī among men,
Vighnavināśinī among the Vināyakas, Jyotis among the Ādityas, Gāndharvī among the Gandharvas, and likewise among the Apsarases.

Thus, Gaurī resides among the Vasus; Kāmyā remains unmanifest among the Antardhānas; and Āvirbhāvatirobhāvā abides in her own station. The Tāmasī, Rājasī, Sāttvikī, and Mānuṣī reside within the yoga of devotion, which is a mass of pure consciousness and whose singular essence is the bliss of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Oṃ, to the self of vital breath—Oṃ Tat Sat Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ—to that self of vital breath, salutations again and again. || 2.3.1 ||
Oṃ, to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Govinda, the beloved of the Gopīs—Oṃ Tat Sat Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ; salutations again and again to Him. || 2 ||
Oṃ, to the self of the downward breath—Oṃ, Tat, Sat, Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to that self of the downward breath, salutations again and again! || 3 ||
Oṃ, to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, to Aniruddha; Oṃ Tat Sat Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ, salutations again and again to Him. || 4 ||
Oṃ, to the self of the diffused breath (vyāna), Oṃ tat sat bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ; salutations again and again to that self of the diffused breath. || 5 ||
Oṃ, to Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rāma; Oṃ Tat Sad Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ, salutations again and again to Him! || 6 ||
Oṃ! To the self of the udāna breath—Oṃ tat sat bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ—to that self of the udāna, salutations again and again. || 7 ||
Oṃ, to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the delighter of Devakī; Oṃ Tat Sat Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ, salutations again and again to Him! || 8 ||
Oṃ, to the self that is the Samāna breath; Oṃ, Tat, Sat, Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ; to that Samāna self, salutations again and again. || 9 ||
Oṃ, to the illustrious Gopāla, who is one's own true nature; Oṃ Tat Sat Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ, salutations again and again to Him! || 2.3.10 ||
Oṃ! To that Gopāla who is the self of primordial nature (pradhāna), who is Oṃ, Tat, Sat, Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to him indeed, salutations again and again. || 11 ||
Oṃ! To that Gopāla who is the self of the senses, who is Oṃ Tat Sat Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ—to him indeed, salutations again and again. || 12 ||
Oṃ! To that very Soul of all beings, Gopāla—Oṃ Tat Sat Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ—to him indeed, salutations again and again. || 13 ||
Oṃ! To that Supreme Person, the Cowherd, Oṃ Tat Sat Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ—to Him indeed, salutation after salutation! || 14 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed the supreme Brahman, the very Brahman—Oṃ Tat Sat Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ—to him, indeed, be salutation after salutation. || 15 ||
Oṃ! To him who is the self of all beings, Gopāla, Oṃ Tat Sat Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ—to him, salutations again and again. || 16 ||
Oṃ! He who transcends the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turiya), the inner controller, Gopāla—Oṃ Tat Sat Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ; salutations again and again to Him. || 17 ||
The one God, hidden in all beings,
all-pervading, the inner self of all beings,
the supervisor of actions, and the abode of all beings.
The witness, the perceiver, absolute and devoid of qualities. || 18 ||
Homage to Rudra. Homage to Āditya. Homage to Vināyaka. Homage to Sūrya. Homage to Vidyā. Homage to Indra. Homage to Agni. Homage to Yama.
Homage to Nirṛti. Homage to Varuṇa. Homage to Vāyu. Homage to Kubera.
"Salutation to Īśāna! Salutation to all the gods!
Having offered this most meritorious hymn of praise to Brahmā, who is his own essential nature, he vanished from the sight of all beings. || 19 ||
"O sage, I have heard this from Nārada regarding Brahmā and the sons of Brahmā;
thus it has been declared, O daughter of the Gandharvas: 'Go now to the vicinity of your own abode. (2.3.20) Thus [it ends].
Oṃ! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O You who are worthy of worship.
With steady limbs and bodies, we have offered praise; may we attain the life-span ordained by the gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being.
May Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are unharmed, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace! Hariḥ Oṃ, that is the Truth.
Thus ends the Gopālottaratāpinī Upaniṣad.
